Where it began

Lala Amarnath was born in Kapurthala, in the Punjab, on 11 September 1911. His talent was spotted in Lahore, and that won him a chance to play in Bombay.

He was a cricketer of many parts. He batted, he bowled, and when needed he even took the gloves, holding five catches as a wicketkeeper in Tests.

The first hundred

England toured India in 1933, and Amarnath made his Test debut against them at the Bombay Gymkhana. In that match he scored the first Test hundred ever made by an Indian, and he ended the series as its leading run-scorer. It was a start few could dream of.

He played only three Tests before a long wartime gap with no official Test cricket, and 21 more after it. In 24 Tests between 1933 and 1952 he scored 878 runs at 24.39, with that famous 118 his only hundred, and took 45 wickets at 32.91. His best bowling was 5 for 96. He also holds a small, unbreakable place in the record books: he was the only bowler to dismiss Don Bradman hit wicket.

Captain of a new nation

When India toured Australia in 1947–1948, Amarnath was the captain, the first to lead the side after independence. He led India in 15 Tests, winning two and drawing seven. The finest moment came at Delhi in 1952, when India beat Pakistan in a Test for the first time and went on to take the series 2–1. He later managed the side on its tour of Pakistan in 1954–55, and he was widely admired for building goodwill between the cricketers and supporters of the two countries.

A Test average in the twenties may look modest for so towering a figure. Then again, few men have been asked to bat, bowl, keep wicket and captain, and at times, it must have felt, all in the same afternoon.

Away from the middle

After his playing days he chaired India's senior selection committee and worked as a commentator and expert. Among his proteges were three men who went on to play for India: Jasu Patel, Chandu Borde and M.L. Jaisimha.

The Government of India gave him the Padma Bhushan in 1991, and he was the first to receive the C. K. Nayudu Lifetime Achievement Award. Two of his sons, Surinder and Mohinder, went on to play Test cricket for India. He died in 2000, aged eighty-eight.

And finally

In the 2021 film 83, the part of Lala Amarnath went to someone who knew him rather well: his son Mohinder. It is hard to imagine better casting.
